behavior_items: The full test defines a global boolean flag initially set to false and a small RAII class C whose constructor saves the old flag value in a data member and then sets the global flag to true. Its destructor restores the previous value. This means that while a local C object is alive, code executed in that scope should observe flag == true, and after scope exit the prior state is restored.

A global replacement operator new(unsigned long) is provided. Before allocating with malloc, it asserts that flag is true. Therefore any allocation performed while a C guard object is alive must succeed, while an allocation performed outside that guarded region would trip the assertion.
A matching global operator delete(void*) calls free. Function g(int* p) simply performs delete p, exercising the normal deallocation path after the guarded allocation has already happened.

Function f() is the core reproducer. It declares an int* p, then enters an inner block, constructs C c, performs p = new int, exits the block so c is destroyed, and finally calls g(p). Semantically, the constructor side effect setting flag = true must occur before the call to operator new, because new int invokes the user-defined allocation function during the lifetime of c.

The object lifetime and sequencing are important. In standard C++ execution, construction of c begins when control enters the block, the constructor writes flag = true, then the new-expression calls operator new, then after the block ends c's destructor restores flag. Thus operator new should always see flag == true in this program.

The reported regression is optimization-sensitive. GCC 10.3 behaves correctly at -O0, -O1, and -O3. GCC 11.1 behaves correctly at -O0 but miscompiles at -O1 and higher, causing the assertion inside operator new to fire. That indicates the source is valid and the failure is introduced by an optimization pass rather than by undefined behavior in the program.

According to the bug report, when the constructor of C is inlined into f, the generated machine code omits the store corresponding to flag = true before the call to operator new. As a result, the allocator still observes the old false value and assert(flag) fails. The compiler is therefore incorrectly eliminating or moving an observable side effect.

This side effect is observable because operator new reads the same global variable. Even though C's constructor and destructor only manipulate a global boolean, those writes cannot be optimized away across the allocation call: the call is not pure, it can read globals, and in this test it explicitly does so. Therefore the reproducer exercises GCC's handling of aliasing/effect modeling around inlined constructors and new-expressions.

The deallocation path through g(p) and operator delete is not what triggers the failure. It exists to make the example complete and leak-free, while also ensuring the allocated pointer escapes the inner block and remains valid until after c is destroyed. The failure occurs earlier, at allocation time, inside operator new.

The minimized reproducer snippet shown separately is incomplete by itself because it omits the declarations of flag, class C, operator new, headers, and helper functions from the bug report. The relevant behavior must therefore be understood from the complete report, where those missing pieces establish the RAII guard and the allocation-time assertion.

In compiler terms, the reproducer stresses preservation of constructor side effects under inlining and optimization, especially across a new-expression that lowers to a call to the replaceable global allocation function. The wrong-code symptom is that GCC 11 optimization treats the constructor write as dead or not needed before the call, which violates C++ observable behavior.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The test uses an RAII guard object C to set a global flag to true for the duration of an inner scope, and a custom global operator new that asserts the flag is true before allocating. In f(), C c is constructed immediately before new int, so correct execution requires the constructor's store to flag to happen before the allocator call. GCC 10.3 and GCC 11.1 at -O0 honor this, but GCC 11.1 at -O1+ reportedly inlines the constructor and then drops the flag-setting store in generated code. That makes operator new observe flag == false and triggers the assertion. The reproducer therefore exercises a regression in optimization of inlined constructor side effects across a new-expression, not a problem in user code semantics.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern is a wrong-code regression introduced only under optimization in GCC 11.1, not at -O0 and not in GCC 10.3. The program relies on a simple RAII guard: the constructor of C writes a global flag before a new-expression, and the destructor restores it after scope exit. A user-defined global operator new reads that same global flag and asserts it is true. Therefore the constructor store is an observable side effect that must be preserved and sequenced before the allocation call. The reported bad codegen specifically says that after inlining C's constructor into f, the store flag = true is missing before operator new executes. This strongly suggests an optimizer defect in side-effect/liveness modeling rather than any issue in source semantics. The common pattern is: inlined constructor with write to global state, immediately followed by a new-expression lowered to a call to replaceable operator new, where GCC incorrectly treats the constructor write as dead, redundant, or movable across the call. Because operator new is an ordinary call that may read globals, any pass that models it too weakly, folds object lifetime too aggressively, or mishandles sequencing around cleanup regions could cause exactly this assertion failure.
possible_causes: Dead store elimination or DSE in SSA/tree optimizers incorrectly removing the constructor's store to the global flag after inlining, because it fails to recognize that the subsequent call to replaceable operator new may read that global.
Call side-effect/escape analysis bug treating operator new or the lowered new-expression as not observing arbitrary global memory, causing motion or elimination of preceding global stores.
Inlining or IPA propagation defect where the inlined constructor body loses required VDEF/memory dependence information, so later optimization sees flag = true as unobservable.
Store sinking/hoisting or code motion bug moving the global flag store past the allocation call or out of the guarded region, violating required sequencing before operator new.

Incorrect interaction between C++ frontend lowering of new-expressions and RAII cleanup/lifetime representation, leading middle-end passes to think the constructor side effect is only relevant to the local object and not to intervening calls.
Alias/mod-ref analysis bug for global variables causing the optimizer to assume the call cannot read flag, even though the user-defined operator new does so explicitly.

EH/cleanup region optimization bug around the inner scope with constructor/destructor, where simplification of the scope or cleanup edges causes the constructor store to be dropped when the constructor is inlined.

Regression in early optimization passes enabled at -O1 (such as early DSE, CCP, FRE, or DOM) that fold the flag value incorrectly across the constructor/new call sequence and delete the write as redundant.
evidence: Bug is optimization-sensitive: GCC 11.1 fails at -O1+ but succeeds at -O0, while GCC 10.3 succeeds at all listed levels, indicating a regression in optimized code generation.
The bug report explicitly states that the store at #1, flag = true in C's constructor, is not emitted in machine code when the constructor is inlined into f.
operator new contains assert(flag), so the constructor's write is externally observable by the very next call and cannot legally be removed.
Program sequencing is straightforward: construct C c, then execute new int while c is alive, then destroy c on block exit. Therefore operator new must see flag == true.
The failure occurs at allocation time inside operator new, not during delete, so the root cause is before or during lowering/optimization of the new-expression.
The manipulated state is a global variable, which makes incorrect DSE/mod-ref/call-clobber reasoning a strong match for the symptom.

The destructor restoring the prior value after the scope means the constructor write is temporary but still required before the call; this is a common pattern that can expose overly aggressive lifetime or store-elimination optimizations.

selected_files.reason: Most directly matches the symptom: an optimized-away global store (`flag = true`) that should remain visible to the immediately following call to user-defined `operator new`. This pass performs tree-level dead store elimination using virtual operands, and a bug here could wrongly conclude the store is dead if call-clobber/read effects for the allocation call are modeled incorrectly.

A wrong-code DSE or code-motion bug here would likely stem from bad alias/mod-ref reasoning. The reproducer depends on GCC understanding that the call to replaceable global `operator new` may read arbitrary global memory, including `flag`; if alias analysis says otherwise, the constructor store can be deleted or moved illegally.

Virtual use/def construction is critical for preserving memory dependencies across calls and global stores. If the inlined constructor store or the `operator new` call is missing the right VUSE/VDEF information, later SSA optimizers could incorrectly treat the store to `flag` as unobservable and eliminate it.

The bug report strongly suggests incorrect modeling of what the allocation call may read or clobber. This file computes mod/ref summaries used by alias analysis and optimization; if `operator new` or the lowered new-expression is inferred too weakly, preceding stores to globals may be optimized away.

If the replaceable global allocation function is mistakenly classified with overly strong purity/const properties, optimizers may assume it does not read global state and thus remove `flag = true`. That is a strong conceptual fit for a regression where a store before a call disappears only under optimization.

C++ `new`-expression and initialization/lifetime lowering live here. Since the reproducer specifically involves constructor inlining immediately before a `new int`, a frontend lowering bug in how the allocation call and object-lifetime sequencing are represented could expose later middle-end passes to an invalid form.

This file bridges C++ frontend semantics into generic/gimple form. The bug involves RAII scope, constructor/destructor sequencing, and a replaceable allocation call; if gimplification loses or weakens the memory side effects of the constructor or new-expression, later optimization could legally-looking but incorrectly remove the store.

The report explicitly says the failure appears when the constructor is inlined into `f`. Inlining must preserve memory effects and sequencing; if inlining of the constructor body loses dependence information for the global store, subsequent optimizers could mis-handle it.

This early optimization pass can remove redundant stores or propagate values aggressively at -O1. A regression here could incorrectly fold the global flag state across the inlined constructor and the allocation call, especially if it relies on flawed call memory information from alias/modref.

General gimplification and statement sequencing are relevant because the bug is about preserving an observable side effect before a call. If the lowered GIMPLE around the inner scope, constructor side effect, or allocation call is malformed, downstream passes such as DOM or DSE could miscompile exactly this pattern.

If FLAGS is LOOKUP_ONLYCONVERTING then it is the = init form of the initializer, if FLAGS is 0, then it is the (init) form. If INIT resolves to a CALL_EXPR which happens to return something of the type we are looking for, then we know that we can safely use that call to perform the initialization. The virtual function table pointer cannot be set up here, because we do not really know its type. This never calls operator=(). When initializing, nothing is CONST. A default copy constructor may have to be used to perform the initialization. A constructor or a conversion operator may have to be used to perform the initialization, but not both, as it would be ambiguous.

FIXME should we complexify the prequeue handling instead? Or use flags for all the cleanups and let the optimizer tighten them up? The current code seems pretty fragile; it will break on a cleanup within any non-conditional nesting. But any such nesting would be broken, anyway; we can't write a TRY_FINALLY_EXPR that starts inside a nesting construct and continues out of it. reviewed_methods.signature: static void dse_optimize_stmt (function *fun, gimple_stmt_iterator *gsi, sbitmap live_bytes)
reviewed_methods.summary: Attempt to eliminate dead stores in the statement referenced by BSI. A dead store is a store into a memory location which will later be overwritten by another store without any intervening loads. In this case the earlier store can be deleted. In our SSA + virtual operand world we use immediate uses of virtual operands to detect dead stores. If a store's virtual definition is used precisely once by a later store to the same location which post dominates the first store, then the first store is dead.
reviewed_methods.reason: Very plausible top-level fix location because it applies DSE decisions and contains the logic that routes stores and calls into the dead-store machinery. If the bug is in the final safety checks or in how this routine handles the constructor store after inlining, the bad deletion would happen here. Slightly less direct than dse_classify_store because this routine mostly orchestrates classification.

If the constructor call or its memory effects are misrepresented here, later DSE or motion could remove flag = true. However, the reproducer is less about object initialization result slots and more about preserving a global store across a following call, so this is somewhat secondary.
